```{r, setup, include=FALSE}
library(mosaic)
library(math260projdata)
```

This sheet collects the R steps you are most likely to need while building your poster. Every box of code can be **copied with the button in its top-right corner** and pasted into your own Quarto file.

The examples use two datasets from `math260projdata`, `coasters` and `happiness`. **Swap in the names of your own dataset and variables** wherever you see them. Names, spelling and capitalization must match your data exactly.

The recipes build on each other in order. If an example uses `coasters2`, it was created in Section 3.

# 1. Look at your data first

Before you filter or recode anything, check what is actually there.

```{r}
head(coasters, n = 3)                # first few rows
names(coasters)                      # variable names
tally(~ material, data = coasters)   # labels of a categorical variable
favstats(~ speed, data = coasters)   # a quantitative variable
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why check labels?
Filtering and recoding only work if you type each category **exactly** as it appears (`"Wooden"`, not `"wooden"`). Use `tally()` to see the exact spelling.
:::

# 2. Filter cases

Filtering keeps only the rows you want. **Always save the result under a new name** (like `steel` below) so your original data stay intact.

**Keep one group**

```{r}
steel <- coasters |> filter(material == "Steel")
```

**Keep two (or more) groups.** Use `%in%` with a list of labels. Add `droplevels()` so the unused category does not linger in tables and graphs.

```{r}
two_types <- coasters |>
  filter(material %in% c("Steel", "Wooden")) |>
  droplevels()
```

**Keep cases that meet a numerical condition.** A comma between conditions means "and".

```{r}
tall_fast <- coasters |> filter(height > 40, speed >= 100)
```

**Look for outliers, then remove one only if you have a reason.**

```{r}
# The five fastest coasters
coasters |> arrange(desc(speed)) |> select(name, speed, height) |> head(n = 5)

# Drop only the 240 km/h coaster, then count the cases before and after
no_outlier <- coasters |> filter(speed < 220)
nrow(coasters)
nrow(no_outlier)
```

**Drop cases with a missing value** for one variable

```{r}
happy_known <- happiness |> filter(!is.na(continent))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Poster tip
Be sure to say on your poster the sample size for the final sample after any removed cases.
:::

# 3. Recode variables

Recoding creates a **new column** with `mutate()`. Most of the course methods compare two groups, so these recipes turn a variable into a two-category variable.

**Categorical to binary: one category versus all the others**

```{r}
coasters2 <- coasters |>
  mutate(wooden = ifelse(material == "Wooden", "Wooden", "Not wooden"))
```

**Quantitative to binary: split at a cutoff you can justify**

```{r}
coasters2 <- coasters2 |>
  mutate(fast = ifelse(speed >= 100, "Fast", "Not fast"))
```

**Collapse several categories into two** (this one uses `happiness`)

```{r}
happiness2 <- happiness |>
  mutate(region2 = ifelse(continent %in% c("Europe", "Americas"), "Europe/Americas", "Other"))
```

**Quantitative to several ordered groups** with `cut()`

```{r}
coasters2 <- coasters2 |>
  mutate(height_group = cut(height, breaks = c(0, 20, 40, Inf),
                            labels = c("Low (up to 20 m)", "Medium (20 to 40 m)", "Tall (over 40 m)")))
```

**Choose which group comes first.** The first level listed comes first in tables and graphs.

```{r}
coasters2 <- coasters2 |>
  mutate(wooden = factor(wooden, levels = c("Wooden", "Not wooden")))
```

**Always check that the recode did what you intended**

```{r}
tally(wooden ~ material, data = coasters2)
tally(fast ~ height_group, data = coasters2)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Keep your data steps together
Put all of your filtering and recoding in one chunk near the top of your Quarto file, and give the final dataset one name. Then your whole analysis re-runs correctly every time you render.
:::

# 4. Numerical summaries and tables

**Compare a quantitative variable across two groups**

```{r}
favstats(speed ~ wooden, data = coasters2)
```

**Difference in group means.** R subtracts the first group's mean from the second's, so this is the mean for "Not wooden" minus the mean for "Wooden". Reverse the order of the levels in Section 3 if you would rather report it the other way.

```{r}
diffmean(speed ~ wooden, data = coasters2)
```

**Compare proportions.** The first table gives conditional proportions for each group. The second gives one proportion.

```{r}
tally(fast ~ wooden, data = coasters2, format = "proportion")
prop(~ fast, data = coasters2, success = "Fast")
```

**A clean table for your poster.** Choose only the columns your audience needs and round them. When you render your Quarto file, you can copy this table from the HTML page and paste it into PowerPoint.

```{r}
favstats(speed ~ wooden, data = coasters2) |>
  select(wooden, n, mean, sd) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

# 5. Graphs for your poster

Pick the tab that matches your variables. Each recipe already includes labels (see the last tab for what each label does).

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Compare groups: histograms

```{r}
gf_histogram(~ speed | wooden ~ ., data = coasters2, binwidth = 10) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Top speeds of wooden and non-wooden coasters",
          x = "Top speed (km/h)", y = "Number of coasters")
```

## Compare groups: boxplots

```{r}
gf_boxplot(speed ~ wooden, data = coasters2) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Wooden coasters tend to be faster",
          x = "Coaster material", y = "Top speed (km/h)")
```

## Two quantitative variables

One overall line:

```{r}
gf_point(speed ~ height, data = coasters2, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_smooth(method = "lm") |>
  gf_labs(title = "Taller coasters are faster",
          x = "Height (meters)", y = "Top speed (km/h)")
```

Color the points by group:

```{r}
gf_point(speed ~ height, data = coasters2, color = ~ wooden, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Speed and height by material",
          x = "Height (meters)", y = "Top speed (km/h)", color = "Material")
```

## Categorical variables

One variable:

```{r}
gf_props(~ material, data = coasters2) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Most coasters in the database are steel",
          x = "Coaster material", y = "Proportion of coasters")
```

Compare groups with stacked bars:

```{r}
gf_props(~ wooden, fill = ~ fast, data = coasters2, position = "fill") |>
  gf_labs(title = "Share of fast coasters, by material",
          x = "Coaster material", y = "Proportion", fill = "Speed")
```

If the category names are long, flip the bars with `gf_refine(coord_flip())` added at the end.

## Labels, size and color

`gf_labs()` can set any of these (use only the ones you need):

```{r}
gf_boxplot(speed ~ wooden, data = coasters2) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Title: state the finding",
          subtitle = "Subtitle: describe the data or sample",
          x = "x-axis label with units",
          y = "y-axis label with units",
          caption = "Source: Captain Coaster community database")
```

**Make text large enough for a poster** by adding `gf_theme()` as the last step:

```{r}
gf_boxplot(speed ~ wooden, data = coasters2) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Wooden coasters tend to be faster",
          x = "Coaster material", y = "Top speed (km/h)") |>
  gf_theme(theme_bw(base_size = 18))
```

**Choose colors.** A `~` before a variable name means "use a different color for each group". Quotes around a color name mean "use this one color for everything".

```{r}
gf_histogram(~ speed, data = coasters2, binwidth = 10, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") |>
  gf_labs(x = "Top speed (km/h)", y = "Number of coasters") |>
  gf_theme(theme_bw(base_size = 18))
```

Type `colors()` at the Console to see the names R knows.

:::

# 6. Save a graph as a PNG for PowerPoint

**Point and click.** Make your graph, then in the **Plots** pane choose **Export → Save as Image**. Pick **PNG**, set the size, and save the file in your project folder. You can also choose **Copy to Clipboard** and paste straight into your poster.

**With code.** Save the graph under a name, then use `ggsave()`. The size is in inches.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
speed_plot <- gf_boxplot(speed ~ wooden, data = coasters2) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Wooden coasters tend to be faster",
          x = "Coaster material", y = "Top speed (km/h)") |>
  gf_theme(theme_bw(base_size = 18))

ggsave("speed_boxplot.png", plot = speed_plot, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

The file is saved in your working directory. Type `getwd()` at the Console to see where that is.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check the size on your poster
Text scales with the image. If the text looks too small after you place the image on your poster, save it again with a smaller `width`/`height` or a larger `base_size`. Resizing the picture in PowerPoint does not fix the text size relative to the rest of the poster.
:::

# 7. Save your cleaned data to a file

To use your filtered or recoded data somewhere else, such as StatKey or Excel, write it to a CSV file. Keeping only the columns you need makes the file easier to work with.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
two_types |>
  select(name, material, speed) |>
  write.csv("coasters_two_types.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

# 8. When something goes wrong

| What you see | What it usually means |
|:-----------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| `object 'xxx' not found` | A typo, or you did not run the chunk that creates it, or you forgot to save a result with `<-` |
| `could not find function "filter"` | The setup chunk with `library(mosaic)` has not been run |
| Zero rows after `filter()` | A category was spelled differently than in the data. Check with `tally()`. Use `==`, not `=` |
| An empty category in a table or graph | Add `|> droplevels()` after your `filter()` |
| `unexpected symbol` or `unexpected ','` | A missing or extra comma, quote or parenthesis. A `|>` goes at the **end** of a line, never the start |
| New column is all `NA` | The old column name or a category label in `ifelse()` is misspelled |
